extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, ornithologists, and students of evolutionary biology
extracted.subtask_description: Use relations among adult male, adult female, and juvenile plumage to classify bird species (Classes I–IV) and to infer the roles of sexual selection, natural selection for protection, transference of characters, and age/sex-limited inheritance in producing sexual differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class I — adult male conspicuous; young resemble adult female
rubrics_metrics.description: When the adult male is brighter or more conspicuous than the adult female, the young of both sexes in their first plumage resemble the adult female.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin: the most obvious conclusion from young and females resembling each other while differing from males is that the males alone have been modified. Examples and supporting observations (parrots, kingfishers, pigeons, Heliothrix, Mergus) are given; representative species across distinct countries often show changed adult males while females and young remain indistinguishable, supporting male-specific modification via sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference: male-only modification indicates sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the young and females closely resemble each other and both differ from the males, infer that the males alone have been modified (e.g., through sexual selection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by cases where males of representative species differ between regions while females and young remain alike; sexual selection acting on male ornaments, with females and young left unchanged, is the parsimonious explanation rather than direct environmental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summer/nuptial plumage as evidence of male sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Closely-allied species may be distinguishable by their summer (nuptial) plumage yet indistinguishable in winter and immature plumage; the nuptial plumage was likely acquired by adult males and modified thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin points to Indian wagtails and Ardeola herons: summer plumes differ between species while winter/immature plumage is common, suggesting nuptial plumage originated in males and was later modified by sexual selection. Use seasonal comparisons to infer ancestral states and sexual selection effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct action of conditions vs selection: subordinate role of direct effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Because females and young, exposed to the same conditions as males, often remain unchanged while males vary, direct action of environmental conditions is generally subordinate to accumulated selection (especially sexual selection) in producing male differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin allows that direct conditions may sometimes act (and could act chiefly on one sex), but emphasizes sexual selection and accumulated variations as the principal causes of the pronounced sexual differences observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transference of characters from males to females
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between females of allied species can often be explained by the partial transference to the female of characters acquired by the males through sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: British finches, many Gallinaceae, Polyplectron. Females often differ chiefly in features in which they partially resemble their respective males. Transference can occur both in ancient and recent times; brilliant colours, however, are transferred much more rarely than other tints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brilliant colours rarely transferred to females (predation and late-acting variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright male colours are less frequently transferred to females than dull tints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes two possible reasons: (1) natural selection may check transfer of bright colours to females exposed to danger during incubation (Wallace's view); (2) variations arising late in life tend to be transmitted only to the same sex (males), so extremely bright tints appearing late would not be passed to females. Use both ecological risk and age-of-expression of variation to explain limited transference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female-limited modification for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Females (and young) may in some instances be modified independently of males for the sake of protection by the accumulation of variations limited in transmission to the female sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin treats this as possible but often doubtful; it would explain dull female colouring without relying on loss via selection or intercrossing. Ground birds (gallinaceous) are possible examples; evidence must be assessed cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-appearing variations transmitted only to adult males (age-limited inheritance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive ornamental variations occurring in males at a rather late age may be transmitted only to adult male offspring, explaining why females and young often remain unmodified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that late-life appearance of variations causes sex-limited transmission, and any similar variations in females/young would be unhelpful or dangerous and thus not selected. This mechanism explains many sex-specific ornaments and why females show partial or no expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class II — adult female more conspicuous; young resemble adult male
rubrics_metrics.description: When the adult female is more conspicuous than the adult male, the young of both sexes in their first plumage resemble the adult male.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cases are rare and the sexual differences are generally less pronounced than in Class I. Examples: certain Turnix species, Painted Snipes (Rhynchaea), some Phalaropus; often associated with reversed roles (female larger, pugnacious) and male incubation. Darwin suggests sexual selection may act on females when they court males or compete for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of reversed sexual selection (female-bright/ male-incubating cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits suggesting sexual selection acting on females include larger and more pugnacious females, females performing courtship/competition for males, and males taking on incubation duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites Turnix (females used for fighting, females associate in flocks), Rhynchaea (females more richly coloured and with masculine tracheal structures), emu and cassowary cases where males incubate. These behavioral and structural correlates support the inference that females can be the target of sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class III — adults alike, young have peculiar first plumage
rubrics_metrics.description: When the adult male resembles the adult female, the young of both sexes have a peculiar first plumage of their own (i.e., young differ from adults).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin interprets this as the young having retained an ancient state of plumage while adults (both sexes) acquired a new coloration—often via sexual selection acting on nearly mature males but transmitted to both sexes at maturity. Examples: robin, scarlet ibis, many herons, swans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class IV — adults alike, young resemble adults in first plumage
rubrics_metrics.description: When adult male and female resemble each other, the young of both sexes in their first plumage resemble the adults (young and adults similar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cases are common (kingfishers, some woodpeckers, jay, magpie, crow, hedge-warbler). Darwin notes similarity between young and adults is seldom complete and graduates into dissimilarity; use degree of resemblance to evaluate timing/transmission of color traits.
